title: Introduction to organic chemistry
learningObjective: know that a hydrocarbon is a compound of hydrogen and carbon only; understand how to represent organic molecules using empirical formulae, molecular formulae, general formulae, structural formulae and displayed formulae; know what is meant by the terms homologous series, functional group and isomerism; understand how to name compounds relevant to this specification using the rules of International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) nomenclature students will be expected to name compounds containing up to six carbon atoms; understand how to write the possible structural and displayed formulae of an organic molecule given its molecular formula; understand how to classify reactions of organic compounds as substitution, addition and combustion knowledge of reaction mechanisms is not required

sections.title: Introduction to organic chemistry
sections.markdown:
Chemistry has two great territories. Everything you studied in the first
three units — metals, salts, acids, the air itself — belongs to the
inorganic half. This chapter opens the other half: the chemistry of
carbon, where sugars, fats and proteins live alongside fuels, plastics,
medicines and dyes. One element builds all of it. Carbon atoms bond to
each other in chains, branched chains and rings, with hydrogen atoms
attached, and the sheer variety of those arrangements is why carbon
chemistry has its own name: **organic chemistry**. Caffeine from a
coffee bean, aspirin from a laboratory bench and the dyes that colour
clothing are all [[organic-compound]]s — carbon compounds with wildly
different sizes and shapes, built from the same bonding rules.

The name has a history worth knowing. *Organic* was originally used
because chemists believed these compounds could only come from living
things. That belief is long gone: organic compounds are made in
factories every day. The modern meaning is precise — an organic
compound is any carbon compound **except the very simplest ones**:
carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, the carbonates and the
hydrogencarbonates stay in the inorganic camp. Within organic
chemistry, the simplest family of all is the [[hydrocarbon]]: a
compound made up of hydrogen and carbon only, and it is where this
chapter's specification statements begin.

Expect a period of adjustment. Organic chemistry greets you with a
crowd of new compounds, unfamiliar names and new ways of drawing
structures — that first impression can be genuinely intimidating, and
this chapter exists to dismantle it. The whole route runs through six
core specification statements, assessed in **both** Paper 1C and Paper
2C, with no chemistry-only band anywhere in Unit 4: what a hydrocarbon
is; the five formula types for representing organic molecules; the
terms homologous series, functional group and isomerism; IUPAC naming
of compounds with up to six carbon atoms; writing possible structures
from a molecular formula; and classifying reactions as substitution,
addition or combustion. Each statement gets its own section or two,
and every skill reappears in later chapters — crude oil, alkanes,
alkenes, alcohols and beyond all run on the machinery you build here.

One practical habit carries more weight than any single fact: get
your hands on molecular models. A school lab will usually have a set;
otherwise modelling clay and matchsticks (or small nails) make
perfectly workable bonds. Physical models let you rotate, twist and
rebuild molecules until the two-dimensional drawings stop looking
arbitrary — and by the time you reach the isomerism sections you will
find the models have quietly done half the teaching. Spend time
exploring: names, structures, models. That is the honest route into
organic chemistry, and every later chapter assumes you took it.

:::prior-knowledge
This chapter assembles tools from earlier units. Covalent bonding and
the four-bond rule for carbon come from Chapter 8 (u1:c08) — displayed
formulae here are just dot-and-cross knowledge drawn with lines.
Empirical and molecular formulae were introduced in Chapter 5 (u1:c05)
and return as two of the five formula types. The covalent bond idea of
shared electron pairs (u1:c03, u1:c08) underpins every line you will
draw. If the four-bond rule or the shared-pair picture feels shaky,
revise those sections first: organic chemistry leans on them in every
section.
:::

:::cross-curricular
Organic chemistry is the chemistry of life and the chemistry of
industry at once. Proteins, sugars and fats — the molecules your body
runs on — are organic. So are the fuels in a camping stove, the
pharmaceuticals in a pharmacy, the dyes in clothing and the plastics
in every device you own. The naming and structure rules in this
chapter are the shared language of medicine, food science, materials
engineering and fuel chemistry; the six-carbon naming limit you will
practise is exactly the vocabulary those industries use daily.
:::

:::exam-hint
Specification wording you can quote: *know that a hydrocarbon is a
compound of hydrogen and carbon only*. Notice the precision — hydrogen
and carbon **only**. A second quotable statement covers the whole
chapter's toolkit: organic molecules are represented using empirical,
molecular, general, structural and displayed formulae. All six
statements in this chapter are non-suffixed core content: they are
shared with Science Double Award and assessed in both Paper 1C and
Paper 2C. There is no Paper-2-only material in this chapter — every
skill here can be tested in either paper.
:::

:::misconception
"Organic means natural, so organic compounds must come from living
things." That was the historical belief, and it is the trap. The modern
definition is structural, not biological: organic compounds are carbon
compounds apart from the very simplest (carbon dioxide, carbon
monoxide, carbonates, hydrogencarbonates). Fertiliser factories,
refineries and pharmaceutical plants synthesise organic compounds on
tonne and milligram scales alike. What excludes a compound from
organic chemistry is its formula — not where it was made.
:::

:::quick-check
Before moving on: can you state what all organic compounds have in
common, and name the four types of carbon compound that stay outside
the organic family? Can you define a hydrocarbon in the examinable
one-clause form? And can you list the six skills this chapter will
build, in order — representation, classification terms, naming,
structure-writing, reaction classes? If any of those wobble, reread
the third paragraph before continuing: the chapter map is also the
revision map.
:::

sections.title: Hydrocarbons
sections.markdown:
Start with the smallest possible organic molecule family. A
[[hydrocarbon]] is a compound that contains carbon and hydrogen
**only** — no oxygen, no halogens, nothing else. The word *only* is
doing real work in that definition, and examiners know it. Virtually
every organic compound contains carbon and hydrogen; what makes a
hydrocarbon special is that carbon and hydrogen are all it contains.
Methane, propane, butane, ethene — the fuels that dominate later
chapters are all hydrocarbons, ranging from single carbon atoms up to
long chains and ring structures, drawn in every arrangement carbon's
four bonds allow.

The carbon atoms in a hydrocarbon chain are joined by single, double
or triple covalent bonds, while every carbon-to-hydrogen bond is a
single bond. That distinction between the carbon-carbon bond types is
not decoration — it splits the whole hydrocarbon family into two
camps. A [[saturated]] hydrocarbon contains only single carbon-carbon
bonds: every carbon uses all four of its bonds on separate partners,
so no more atoms can be added. An [[unsaturated]] hydrocarbon contains
at least one double or triple carbon-carbon bond, and those spare
bonding capacity points are exactly where later reactions happen.
The alkane family (Chapter 24, u4:c24) and the alkene family
(Chapter 25, u4:c25) give each camp its full treatment; here you only
need the vocabulary and the bond-counting logic behind it.

Keep the definition in its examinable shape. If a question shows you a
molecule's structure and asks whether it is a hydrocarbon, the check
is a two-element audit: carbon present, hydrogen present, and
**nothing else**. A molecule like ethanol — which contains an oxygen
atom in its −OH group — fails that audit no matter how carbon-rich it
looks. That audit is also your first classification tool: the next
sections build the formula vocabulary that lets you record what a
molecule contains, and the camp it belongs to.

:::key-point
Organic compounds can be described as **saturated** (containing only
single C–C bonds) or **unsaturated** (containing double or triple C–C
bonds). The two words describe bonding capacity, not reactivity in
general — and the alkane and alkene chapters (u4:c24, u4:c25) develop
exactly how each camp behaves.
:::

:::exam-hint
The definition has a habit of being tested with a near-miss. Carbon
dioxide contains carbon — but no hydrogen, so it is not a hydrocarbon.
Ethanol contains both carbon and hydrogen — but also oxygen, so it is
not a hydrocarbon either. When the specification says *a compound of
hydrogen and carbon only*, the *only* is the mark. Write the full
definition, never "a compound containing hydrogen and carbon", and the
near-misses cannot touch you.
:::

:::misconception
"Organic compound and hydrocarbon mean the same thing." They do not —
hydrocarbon is the strict subset. Every hydrocarbon is an organic
compound, but the reverse fails the moment any third element appears:
alcohols, carboxylic acids and esters all contain oxygen and all sit
outside the hydrocarbon family. If a question asks whether a molecule
is a hydrocarbon, run the two-element audit — carbon, hydrogen,
nothing else — and answer from the audit, not from vibes.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you define a hydrocarbon with the word *only* in place, and
explain why ethanol fails the definition while propane passes it? Can
you say what bond type separates saturated from unsaturated
hydrocarbons, and name the two families (met later) that embody each
camp? If the audit habit — carbon, hydrogen, nothing else — feels
automatic, you are ready for the formula section.
:::

sections.title: Types of formula for organic molecules
sections.markdown:
Organic chemistry needs more than one way to write a molecule down,
because different jobs need different information. The five
representations in specification 4.2 — empirical, molecular, general,
structural and displayed formulae — are not five levels of difficulty;
they are five lenses, and this section installs the first two. An
[[empirical-formula]] shows the **simplest whole-number ratio** of the
atoms in a compound, and it is the version you can calculate from
experimental data (the Chapter 5, u1:c05 toolkit). On its own it
cannot identify the molecule: without more information you cannot
recover the true formula from the ratio alone. Methane's empirical
formula is CH₄ — which happens to be its molecular formula too. But
ethane's empirical formula is CH₃, while its molecular formula is
C₂H₆.

A [[molecular-formula]] counts the **actual number** of each type of
atom in one molecule. Butane is C₄H₁₀; ethene is C₂H₄. Every molecular
formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula: a
compound with empirical formula CH₂ could have molecular formula
C₂H₄, C₃H₆ or C₄H₈ — the carbon-to-hydrogen ratio must always match
the ratio in the empirical formula. That multiplicity is exactly why
the empirical formula alone cannot pin a molecule down.

Here is the limitation that shapes everything else in this chapter: a
molecular formula tells you **nothing** about how the atoms are joined
together. Two completely different compounds can share one molecular
formula — the isomerism section (s09) makes that idea concrete. In
practice, molecular formulae are used rarely in organic chemistry,
precisely because they carry no bonding information. The one place
they earn their keep is combustion equations for simple hydrocarbons,
where the internal structure genuinely does not matter:

2C₄H₁₀(g) + 13O₂(g) → 8CO₂(g) + 10H₂O(l)

In almost every other situation — naming, drawing, predicting
reactions — you will reach for a structural or a displayed formula
instead. Those two, plus the general formula that unites whole
families, are the subjects of the next two sections.

:::exam-hint
The formula-type definitions are quotable, and the ratio check is a
one-mark staple: given molecular formula C₄H₈, the empirical formula
is CH₂ (divide through by the largest whole number possible). More
features of homologous series — the family vocabulary these formulae
feed into — are collected in the alkanes chapter (u4:c24). If a
question asks *which* formula tells you how atoms are joined, the
answer is never the molecular formula: it is the structural or
displayed formula.
:::

:::misconception
"The empirical formula and molecular formula are always different
formulae." Methane breaks that rule on sight: its simplest ratio CH₄
is already the true formula, so the two coincide. The general law is
the multiple — the molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the
empirical formula, and that multiple can be 1. Check by dividing the
subscripts by their largest common factor; if nothing divides, the
formulae are identical.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you define empirical formula (ratio) and molecular formula
(actual counts) in one sentence each? Given CH₂ as an empirical
formula, can you write three valid molecular formulae whose
carbon-to-hydrogen ratio matches it? Can you name the one reaction
type where molecular formulae are actually convenient, and explain
why structure-free formulae are fine there? If yes, the family
vocabulary is next.
:::

sections.title: Homologous series and functional groups
sections.markdown:
Before the third and fourth formula types, you need the family idea
that organises the whole of organic chemistry. Carbon always forms
four bonds and hydrogen always forms one; oxygen forms two and a
halogen atom forms one (that is covalent-bonding bookkeeping from
Chapter 8, u1:c08, not a new rule). With those counts fixed, organic
compounds fall into families — many different families, called
**homologous series**. The alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, carboxylic
acids and esters are all homologous series, each developed in its own
later chapter; the family idea itself is one of the three terms in
specification 4.3.

A [[homologous-series]] is a series of compounds with **similar
chemical properties because they share the same functional group**,
and consecutive members differ from the next by exactly one −CH₂−
unit. That single sentence packs three membership tests: similar
chemistry (same group), the same functional group throughout, and the
−CH₂− step between neighbours. The third test is what makes a
**general formula** possible — a [[general-formula]] writes every
member of the family at once using n for the carbon count. For the
alkanes, a molecule with n carbons always carries 2n + 2 hydrogens,
so the general formula is CnH2n+2. Test it: methane, n = 1, gives
2 × 1 + 2 = 4 hydrogens (CH₄); propane, n = 3, gives 8 (C₃H₈); and
dodecane, n = 12, must carry 2 × 12 + 2 = 26 hydrogens, giving
C₁₂H₂₆ — no experiment needed, just the formula. Different families
have different general formulae: CnH2n for the alkenes, CnH2n+2O for
the alcohols. The first few members sit side by side in the table
below, and you should read each column top-to-bottom watching the
−CH₂− steps happen.

| Alkanes | Alkenes | Alcohols |
|---------|---------|----------|
| CH₄ | — | CH₄O |
| C₂H₆ | C₂H₄ | C₂H₆O |
| C₃H₈ | C₃H₆ | C₃H₈O |
| C₄H₁₀ | C₄H₈ | C₄H₁₀O |

(Read the alkene column's empty first cell as chemistry, not damage: a
double bond needs *two* carbon atoms, so no one-carbon alkene exists.
Every alkane and alcohol count is valid from one carbon upward.)

A [[functional-group]] is an atom or a group of atoms that **determines
the chemical properties** of a compound. All compounds in the same
homologous series carry the same functional group — the −OH group for
alcohols, the C=C double bond for alkenes. One way to think about it:
the functional group is what makes a particular compound behave
differently from an alkane of similar size. The hydrocarbon skeleton
is inert scenery; the group is where the reactions happen.

The last two formula types appear here and get their full treatment in
the next section. A **structural formula** shows how the atoms in a
molecule are joined together, and it comes in two forms: the
**displayed formula** (sometimes called the full structural formula),
which draws every bond as an individual line, and the **condensed
structural formula**, which writes out the chain without bond lines —
propane as CH₃CH₂CH₃. Each line in a displayed formula represents a
pair of shared electrons: a covalent bond, exactly as in Chapter 8.
Displayed formulae are always drawn with the molecule straightened out
and flattened; they do not show the real three-dimensional angles, but
they show exactly how every atom is joined. For butane, the drawn
right-angle appearance has nothing to do with the true shape — in
reality the bonds are arranged tetrahedrally at about 109.5°, the same
geometry that builds the diamond structure you met in u1:c08.

:::maths-skills
The general formula is an arithmetic machine. Given CnH2n+2: n = 1 →
CH₄ (2 × 1 + 2 = 4); n = 3 → C₃H₈ (2 × 3 + 2 = 8); n = 12 → C₁₂H₂₆
(2 × 12 + 2 = 26). The same substitution works for alkenes (CnH2n:
n = 2 → C₂H₄) and alcohols (CnH2n+2O: n = 2 → C₂H₆O). Exam questions
love the reverse direction — "dodecane has 12 carbons; write its
formula" — and the whole trick is trusting the algebra over the
temptation to count hydrogens one by one.
:::

:::exam-hint
The homologous-series definition earns marks in three clauses, so
quote all three: similar chemical properties, *because* they share
the same functional group, differing by −CH₂− between consecutive
members. A question asking "why do all alcohols react similarly?"
wants the functional-group clause, not a list of alcohols. And if you
are asked what makes alcohols different from alkanes, the answer is
the group — −OH — not a property.
:::

:::misconception
"A general formula is just a vague molecular formula." The two answer
different questions. A molecular formula describes *one* molecule —
C₃H₈ is propane, full stop. A general formula describes *every member
of a family at once* — CnH2n+2 is methane, ethane, propane and every
other alkane, with n as the free variable. Confusing them inverts the
whole family idea: the general formula is the pattern, the molecular
formula is one instantiation of it.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you state the three membership tests for a homologous series? Can
you use CnH2n+2 to write the formula for a 12-carbon alkane without
counting hydrogens individually? Can you name the functional group of
the alcohols and of the alkenes, and say in one sentence what a
functional group does? Can you explain why the alkene column of the
table starts at two carbons? Those four checks are the section — pass
them and the drawing section is pure technique.
:::

sections.title: Drawing and using structural formulae
sections.markdown:
For anything larger than the smallest molecules, a fully displayed
formula is time-consuming to draw, so chemistry uses a set of
simplifications — all of them still [[structural-formula]]e, all of
them still showing exactly how the atoms join. You can write a chain
using grouped labels: CH₃ or CH₂ standing in for a carbon with its
attached hydrogens, instead of drawing every carbon-hydrogen bond.
The butane molecule (molecular formula C₄H₁₀ — a [[molecular-formula]]
that alone tells you nothing about joining) can be written as
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ or as CH₃−CH₂−CH₂−CH₃. Both condensed forms show exactly
how the four carbons link in a chain; the molecular formula does not.

The displayed [[displayed-formula]] draws every bond as a line, and
several different-looking drawings can all be correct. Twist a butane
chain in the middle and you have not made a new molecule — the chain
has simply rotated, because rotation around single carbon-carbon
bonds happens freely in real molecules too. Molecular models make
this vivid: blobs of modelling clay joined by matchstick "bonds" will
twist into every drawn arrangement without any bond breaking. By
convention you draw the structure with all carbon atoms in a
straight line, which is why textbook drawings look flatter than the
molecules they describe.

Double bonds follow the same logic with one extra line. Propene,
C₃H₆, contains a carbon-carbon double bond, drawn as **two lines**
between the two carbon atoms — two pairs of shared electrons, the
C=C you met as the alkenes' functional group in s04. You would
normally write propene in a simplified condensed form as CH₃CH=CH₂,
with the double bond shown. More advanced shorthand sometimes hides
the C=C bond inside an abbreviated written formula; at International
GCSE you should always show it. (The same display discipline applies
to writing structure in equations: any unambiguous structural version
is acceptable — but in the drawn-answer cases below, the safest habit
is the full displayed formula.)

:::key-point
If you are asked to **draw** the structure of a molecule in an
International GCSE exam, always draw it as a displayed formula. You
cannot lose marks for showing every bond, whereas a condensed
shorthand can cost you. When you are simply writing a structure
inside an equation, either version is fine — choose whichever you
write fastest without errors.
:::

:::key-point
The boundary between the two structural forms is a bond count. If
**all** the bonds are shown as lines, it is a displayed formula. If
**not all** of them are shown — but the joining is still
unambiguous — it is a (condensed) structural formula. Some condensed
forms show some bonds (CH₃−CH₂−CH₃), others none (CH₃CH₂CH₃); both
are structural, neither is displayed.
:::

:::exam-hint
Models are not exam furniture, they are thinking tools — and rotation
is the idea they teach best. If two drawn structures differ only by a
twist of the chain, they are the same molecule, because single bonds
rotate. Test any "are these the same or different?" question by
asking: could I turn the first drawing into the second without
breaking a bond? If yes, same molecule; if no, different molecule —
and that question is exactly what the isomerism section formalises.
:::

:::worked-example
Draw the displayed formula of propene, CH₃CH=CH₂ (4.5: write the
displayed formula given the molecular formula).

1. Place the three carbons in a line, in the order the condensed
   formula reads: C1, C2, C3.
2. Draw the double bond (two lines) between C1 and C2 — the formula
   says the C=C sits at the start of the chain.
3. Add hydrogens until every carbon has exactly four bonds: C1 takes
   two H atoms (double bond uses two of its four bonds), C2 takes
   one H, C3 takes three H.
4. Audit the count: three carbons, and 2 + 1 + 3 = 6 hydrogens —
   matching C₃H₆. The two-lines rule and the four-bond rule between
   them guarantee the drawing is correct.
:::

:::misconception
"Two structures that look different must be different molecules."
Appearance is not identity in organic chemistry: chains twist, and
single-bond rotation changes the drawing without changing the
molecule. The test is bonding, not layout — same atoms, same
connections, same molecule. Only when bonds would have to **break**
to convert one drawing into the other are you looking at genuinely
different structures (the isomerism idea, two sections ahead).
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write butane in condensed form two different ways and say why
both mean the same molecule? Can you state the all-bonds rule that
separates displayed from condensed structural formulae? Can you draw
propene's displayed formula from its condensed form, using the
four-bond audit to check your hydrogen count? And can you explain
why drawing a twisted chain does not create a new substance? If all
four are secure, naming is next.
:::

sections.title: Naming organic compounds
sections.markdown:
Organic names look complicated until you see that they are **codes**.
[[iupac-nomenclature]] — the naming rules of the International Union
of Pure and Applied Chemistry — builds every name from parts, and each
part tells you something specific: one part gives the number of carbon
atoms in the longest chain, another says whether carbon-carbon double
bonds are present, another identifies branches and functional groups.
Read the parts and the molecule assembles itself; this section
installs the first code book, the chain-length code.

| Code letters | Carbons in chain |
|--------------|------------------|
| meth         | 1                |
| eth          | 2                |
| prop         | 3                |
| but          | 4                |
| pent         | 5                |
| hex          | 6                |

The first four codes have to be learned outright — there is no
pattern connecting one to five to carbon counts. A mnemonic helps:
**M**onkeys **E**at **P**ink **B**ananas lines meth, eth, prop, but
up in order, and the specification's own limit (compounds containing
up to six carbon atoms) means this six-row table is the complete code
book. From five onward the Greek roots take over, which is why *pent*
means five (as in pentagon) and *hex* means six (as in hexagon) —
those two you can reconstruct instead of memorise. Worked examples:
butane carries a chain of four carbon atoms; propane carries a chain
of three.

A second code segment appears inside longer names: the letters *an*
signal that the carbons are joined by **single bonds**. Decode
propan-1-ol as a demonstration: *prop* says three carbon atoms,
*an* says they are joined by carbon-carbon single bonds, and the
ending *-ol* (a code you meet properly in the alcohols section) adds
information of its own. Every extra fragment in a name is a extra
fact about the structure — nothing in an IUPAC name is decoration.

One caution before moving on: the name describes the molecule's
connectivity, not its drawing's orientation. Take but-1-ene drawn
with the double bond at the left, then drawn flipped so it sits on
the right — the same molecule, turned over, with what was left now on
the right and vice versa. Nobody renames a molecule because it moved;
both drawings are but-1-ene. So when two drawings seem to disagree,
check whether a rotation explains the difference before you suspect
two different compounds — and keep the chain-length code (the table
above) as your first decoding stop in every name you meet.

:::exam-hint
Decode-first is the examinable direction. Decoding a name into a
structure is worth far more marks than constructing a name from a
structure, and if you cannot decode what an examiner or a question is
talking about, the whole item is lost — so drill the code table until
meth-through-hex are reflexes. The six-carbon limit is itself a gift:
it caps the vocabulary you must learn and tells you no question will
hide a heptane at you.
:::

:::misconception
"Flipping the drawing changes the name." A molecule in space has no
left or right — the name encodes structure, not page position. But-1-ene
stays but-1-ene whichever end you draw it from, because flipping is
rotation, not reconstruction. The names that genuinely differ (but-1-ene
versus but-2-ene, say) differ in *code content* — where the double
bond starts — never in how the paper is oriented.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you recite the six chain-length codes and their carbon counts,
and say which four need pure memorisation? Can you decode propan-1-ol
fragment by fragment — chain length, bond type, and what the ending
contributes? Can you explain why a molecule drawn upside-down keeps
its name? With the code book installed, the next section adds the
bond-type endings and builds the two simplest families.
:::

sections.title: Alkanes and alkenes
sections.markdown:
The two simplest [[homologous-series]] of hydrocarbons — and the two
endings that will meet you in every organic name — are the alkanes and
the alkenes. **Alkanes** are a homologous series of similar
[[hydrocarbon]]s (compounds of carbon and hydrogen only) in which
every carbon is joined to the next by **single covalent bonds**. The
ending *ane* codes that all-single-bond structure: ethane is a
two-carbon chain (*eth*) with carbon-carbon single bonds, CH₃CH₃ —
the s02 saturated camp, family-sized.

**Alkenes** are a homologous series of hydrocarbons that contain a
**carbon-carbon double bond**, coded in the name by the ending *ene*.
Ethene is a two-carbon chain containing C=C, CH₂=CH₂ — the
unsaturated camp. With longer chains a new question appears: the
double bond could sit anywhere along the chain, and *ene* alone no
longer pins the structure down. The fix is a position number. Number
the chain and state which carbon atom the double bond **starts** at,
written between hyphens in the name:

| Formula | Name | Description |
|---------|------|-------------|
| CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ | but-1-ene | a four-carbon chain with the double bond starting on the first carbon |
| CH₃CH=CHCH₃ | but-2-ene | a four-carbon chain with the double bond starting on the second carbon |

Both molecules are C₄H₈ — the code number, not the formula, is what
distinguishes them. But-1-ene and but-2-ene are genuinely different
compounds: converting one into the other would mean breaking bonds
and rebuilding the chain, not bending it.

One rule fixes the numbering direction: **number from the end that
produces the smaller numbers in the name**. Counting from the left of
CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ puts the double bond at carbon 1; counting from the
right would put it at carbon 3 — and 1 beats 3, so the name is
but-1-ene, not but-3-ene. The same smaller-number principle returns
in the next section for branch positions, so install it once here
and reuse it everywhere.

:::exam-hint
Two names with the same molecular formula are a classic contrast
question: but-1-ene and but-2-ene share C₄H₈ but differ in double-bond
position, and the mark sits on saying the position — first carbon
versus second carbon — precisely. When you write position-coded names
yourself, show the hyphens (but-1-ene, never but1ene): the number is
a separate code element, and its placement carries the information.
:::

:::misconception
"But-1-ene and but-2-ene are the same molecule drawn from different
ends." Flipping a molecule is rotation (s06) — but moving the double
bond is reconstruction. The two alkenes differ in which carbons share
the double bond; no rotation converts one into the other, so they are
distinct compounds. The decoder that separates them is the number in
the name: *-1-* versus *-2-*. Position codes carry structural truth;
orientation carries none.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you define alkane and alkene in one sentence each — series
membership, bond type, and name ending? Can you write ethane and
ethene in condensed form and point at the bond difference? Given
CH₃CH=CHCH₃, can you name it with the correct position number and
justify the numbering direction with the smaller-numbers rule? Those
are the family basics; the next section adds branches to the chain.
:::

sections.title: Branched chains and decoding names
sections.markdown:
Carbon chains grow side branches as well as length, and the naming
code handles branches with exactly the same economy. Hydrocarbon
chains can carry small side chains — at International GCSE you are
likely to meet only two:

| Side chain | Coded |
|------------|-------|
| CH₃−       | methyl |
| CH₃CH₂−    | ethyl  |

The count of carbons in a side chain is coded exactly like a main
chain — *meth* for a one-carbon side chain, *eth* for two — and the
ending **yl** signals that the group is attached to something else
rather than standing alone. A methyl branch is a CH₃ group hanging
off the main chain; an ethyl branch adds one more carbon.

Reading the full [[iupac-nomenclature]] code is a skill worth over-practising, because it is
much more important to be able to **decode** names into structures
than the reverse — if you cannot decode what a question or an examiner
is talking about, you are completely lost. Three rules run the decode.
First, the name of a molecule is always based on the **longest chain**
you can find in it. Second, the position of each branch is numbered
from the end that produces the smaller numbers — exactly as with
double-bond positions in alkenes. Third, when there is more than one
branch, you describe the position of each.

Watch the rules produce two names. The longest chain in the first
molecule has four carbon atoms (*but*) with no double bonds (*ane*),
so the name is based on butane; a methyl group branches from carbon
number 2, counting from the end that gives the smaller number — the
compound is **2-methylbutane**. The second molecule's longest chain
has three carbons and no double bonds, so the base is propane; there
are **two** methyl groups attached to the second carbon — the compound
is **2,2-dimethylpropane**. The prefix *di* shows two identical
branches, and the 2,2 says both sit on the second carbon atom.

Decoding runs in reverse too, and it is specification 4.5's skill:
draw the structure from the name.

:::worked-example
Decode 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene into a [[structural-formula]] (4.4 + 4.5).

1. Scan for the longest-chain code: *but* — a four-carbon main chain.
2. Scan for the bond ending: *ene* with position −2− — a carbon-carbon
   double bond starting on the second carbon atom.
3. Scan for branches: *dimethyl* — two methyl (CH₃) groups, at
   positions 2 and 3.
4. Draw the skeleton first: four carbons in a line, the double bond
   between C2 and C3, a CH₃ branch pointing off C2 and another off
   C3 (up or down does not matter).
5. Add hydrogens last, enough that every carbon makes exactly four
   bonds. Figure-free, formula-first: the name is now a structure —
   and the four-bond audit (u1:c08 bookkeeping) is the check that
   catches every mistake.
:::

:::key-point
Side-chain carbons are counted with the same code as main chains:
*meth* = one carbon, *eth* = two. The ending **yl** is the marker that
the group is attached to something else — methyl is CH₃− *as a
branch*, never methane loose in the mixture.
:::

:::exam-hint
Structure-from-name is where decoding pays its marks: scan the name in
order — longest chain, bond ending and position, branches and their
positions — and build the skeleton before adding any hydrogens. For
the reverse direction, always name from the *longest* chain you can
trace, and remember the branch positions must come out as small
numbers. Draw your isomers with the longest chain horizontal (or
redraw without the hydrogens first) so you never mistake a rotated
chain for a new structure.
:::

:::misconception
"2,2-dimethylpropane must have a five-carbon main chain — I can see
five carbons." Five carbons exist in the molecule, but the **longest
chain** through it holds three: the central carbon connects to four
methyl groups, and any path through the molecule passes three of them.
The name is built on propane with two methyl branches, not on a
five-chain that does not exist. Longest-chain-first is the rule that
makes the code unambiguous — it is why two chemists looking at the
same molecule write the same name.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you decode 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane into structures,
saying which end you numbered from and why? Can you explain what the
*yl* ending adds, and what *di* contributes in a name like
2,2-dimethylpropane? Can you state the three decode rules and run
them on 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene without looking? That last skill — the
worked example — is the examinable centrepiece of this section.
:::

sections.title: Structural isomerism
sections.markdown:
A straight chain is an unbranched chain — that vocabulary point clears
the way for the third big term of specification 4.3. **Structural
[[isomerism]]** exists because one [[molecular-formula]] can clothe
itself in more than one structure: structural isomers are molecules
with the **same molecular formula but different
[[structural-formula]]e**. The atoms in different isomers are joined in a different
order. Examples make it real.

Pick up five carbon atoms and twelve hydrogen atoms — physically, as
molecular models — and try to join them. You will find more than one
way to do it, and every arrangement you build is a legitimate
molecule. All of them have the molecular formula C₅H₁₂; each has a
different structure. There are **three** isomers in the set:

- **pentane** — the straight-chain (unbranched) isomer, five carbons
  in a row;
- **2-methylbutane** — a four-carbon chain (*butane*) with one methyl
  group on the second carbon;
- **2,2-dimethylpropane** — a three-carbon chain (*propane*) with two
  methyl groups on the second carbon, the *di* marking the pair.

The naming you built in s08 now does real work: each isomer's name is
a complete structural report. And there is a physical test hiding in
the model exercise: try converting one isomer into another by bending
or twisting. It cannot be done. Bending and rotating never convert an
isomer — you would have to **break bonds** and reconnect the atoms.
That break-a-bond test is the simplest isomer check you own: same
formula, no rotation route, different connection pattern — isomers.

Students hunting a fourth C₅H₁₂ isomer frequently produce one, and it
is always the same disappointment: the "new" drawing is 2-methylbutane
rotated in space. Guard against the illusion by always drawing isomers
with the longest carbon chain horizontal (or by redrawing the set
without hydrogen atoms first) — then the duplicates expose themselves.
In an exam, show the hydrogens even though the carbon-skeleton sketch
is the faster comparison tool.

:::key-point
Warning: **isomer** and **isotope** are different words for unrelated
ideas. Isotopes are different atoms of the *same element* — same
atomic number, different mass numbers. Isomers are *different
compounds* — same molecular formula, different structural formulae.
One is a contrast within an element; the other is a contrast between
whole molecules. Keep them apart in every answer.
:::

:::exam-hint
Isomer-count questions reward method over inspiration: fix the
molecular formula, then vary chain length, then vary branch positions
(and for alkenes, double-bond position — next section). To compare
candidates quickly, redraw each as a carbon skeleton only — hydrogens
omitted — so duplicates and rotations become visible at a glance.
Then, before writing the final answer, redraw with all hydrogens
shown: the exam wants complete structures, and the four-bond audit is
your self-check.
:::

:::misconception
"I found a fourth isomer of C₅H₁₂." You found a rotation. Every
apparent fourth member of the set is 2-methylbutane seen from a new
angle — same connections, same molecule. The break-a-bond test
settles it: if no bond must break to superimpose the drawings, they
are one compound, not two. Draw the longest chain horizontal every
time and the phantom isomer never appears again.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you state the structural-isomerism definition in its two halves
(same formula, different structure)? Can you draw and name all three
C₅H₁₂ isomers, identifying the longest chain each name is built on?
Can you run the break-a-bond test and explain why rotation never
produces a new isomer? And can you say precisely how an isomer
differs from an isotope? If those four hold, the enrichment section
on mirror-image isomerism is next.
:::

sections.title: Looking ahead: optical isomerism
sections.markdown:
Enrichment section: the isomerism in specification 4.3 is the
structural kind you met in s09, and that is the kind the papers test.
But the word *isomerism* hides a second world, and one glance at it
will make the structural version feel like solid ground. To be
precise, what you have studied should be called **structural
isomerism** — same molecular formula, different structural formulae,
atoms joined in a different order. The other important kind of [[isomerism]] is
**optical isomerism**, and it inverts the premise: optical isomers
have their atoms joined in the **same** order (identical structural
formulae) but arranged differently in three-dimensional space.

They are mirror images of each other — and, like your two hands, they
cannot be superimposed. Rotate one as you like, and it never lies
flat on top of the other: every alignment that matches one part
misaligns another. Optical isomerism appears when a molecule contains
a **chiral centre** — a carbon atom connected to four *different*
atoms or groups. The tetrahedral shape around that carbon (the
molecular geometry you met with diamond in u1:c08) is what locks the
mirror-image arrangement in place: rotate one molecule 180° in space
and it still refuses to stack on its twin.

Here is the strange part: optical isomers have identical chemical
properties — **except when they interact with something else that is
chiral**. Biology is chiral through and through. Apart from glycine,
every naturally occurring amino acid exists in both optical forms,
which means every protein in your body is built from one-handed
building blocks — so your body's receptors can tell the two versions
of a molecule apart. The same compound can smell of spearmint in one
form and of caraway seed in the other, purely because the two mirror
images fit differently into the chiral protein receptors in your
nose.

That asymmetry is not a curiosity — it is a safety-critical fact of
pharmaceutical chemistry. In the 1960s, a drug molecule was given to
pregnant women to treat morning sickness because one of its optical
isomers had anti-nausea effects; unknown to everyone at the time, the
manufacture also produced the mirror-image isomer, and that other
form caused severe limb deformities in thousands of children. The
thalidomide tragedy rewrote the industry's rulebook: drug companies
now spend heavily on separating the optical isomers of every new
chiral drug, in case one form carries side effects the other does
not. One molecule, two mirror images, two biological fates — the
cleanest possible demonstration that in chemistry, structure is
meaning. (Extension, beyond even the main line here: the two forms
of a chiral molecule are labelled with the prefixes R and S to record
the configuration of atoms around the chiral centre.)

:::exam-hint
Keep the two isomerisms straight by their one-line signatures:
structural isomers differ in **bonding order**; optical isomers
differ in **three-dimensional arrangement** only. For International
GCSE, "isomerism" in specification 4.3 means the structural kind —
same formula, different structures, break-a-bond test (s09). Optical
isomerism is beyond-the-paper enrichment, but the chiral-centre idea
— a carbon with four different groups — is a beautiful application of
the tetrahedral carbon geometry you already own.
:::

:::misconception
"Mirror images are just the same molecule seen from the other side."
For a chiral molecule, no rotation ever superimposes the two forms —
that refusal is the definition. The consequences are chemical, not
philosophical: one form of carvone smells of spearmint, its mirror
image of caraway; one form of a drug treats nausea, its mirror image
caused a tragedy. Same connections, different space — different
compound in every way that biology can detect.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you say what structural isomerism and optical isomerism each
compare, in one line each? Can you define a chiral centre and explain
why four different groups around a tetrahedral carbon produce
non-superimposable mirror images? Can you state when optical isomers'
chemical properties differ — and why your nose can tell them apart?
Then continue: the alkene isomers are waiting, and they are fully
examinable.
:::

sections.title: Ethene, propene and the alkene isomers
sections.markdown:
Apply the isomer machinery to the smallest alkenes and the pattern
snaps into focus. Ethene, CH₂=CH₂, has **no isomers** — with only two
carbons there is nowhere else for anything to go. Propene,
CH₃CH=CH₂, almost has one: you can move atoms around, but there is no
rearrangement of C₃H₆ that still contains a carbon-carbon double bond
in a chain. So propene has no structural isomer that is still an
alkene.

The [[molecular-formula]], though, keeps its options open. There is a
structural isomer of C₃H₆ that contains **no** carbon-carbon double
bond at all: three carbon atoms joined in a **ring**. It is called
cyclopropane, and the name is itself a decode — a ring of three
carbons with only single bonds between them. Each ring carbon bonds
to its two ring neighbours, using two of its four bonds, and to two
hydrogens for the rest: C₃H₆ exactly. Cyclopropane and propene are
genuine structural [[isomerism]] cases — same molecular formula, different
structural formulae (ring versus chain), and the break-a-bond test
from s09 confirms no rotation converts one into the other. (This ring
versus chain contrast is extension material: the examinable skill is
the isomer definition, and cyclopropane is its most surprising
demonstration.)

Move up to C₄H₈ and the double-bond set grows to **three** structural
isomers that each contain a carbon-carbon double bond: but-1-ene,
but-2-ene, and 2-methylpropene — a branched three-carbon chain with
the double bond in the middle. Notice the two independent dials you
are turning: the **position** of the double bond along the chain
(but-1-ene versus but-2-ene) and the **branching** of the chain
(2-methylpropene). Isomer enumeration at this level is just running
those dials systematically — fix the formula, walk through chain
lengths, branch positions and double-bond positions, and discard
rotations along the way.

:::exam-hint
"What isomers exist with molecular formula X?" is a specification 4.5
question, and the method is dial-walking: every alkene isomer must
contain C=C, so enumerate chain lengths, branch patterns and
double-bond positions, then strike out duplicates that differ only by
rotation. For C₃H₆ the examinable answer inside the alkene camp is
"propene only" — but knowing cyclopropane exists shows the examiner
you understand that the formula, not the functional group, defines
the isomer set.
:::

:::misconception
"A ring molecule can't be an isomer of a chain molecule — one has a
double bond and the other doesn't." The isomer test never mentions
functional groups: same molecular formula, different structural
formula, different compound. Propene (C₃H₆, chain, C=C) and
cyclopropane (C₃H₆, ring, all single bonds) pass the test exactly.
The formula is the identity card; where the bonds go is the
difference.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you explain why ethene has no isomers and propene has none within
the alkene family? Can you decode the name cyclopropane into a ring
structure and show it is C₃H₆? Can you name the three alkene isomers
of C₄H₈, saying which dial each one turns? With the isomer toolkit
complete, one more family gets a first look before the chapter closes
— the alcohols.
:::

sections.title: A first look at the alcohols
sections.markdown:
One more family gets a first look before this chapter closes — the
alcohols, because they will meet you again in the reactions section
and at full length in a later chapter. **Alcohols** are a
[[homologous-series]] of compounds which all contain an **−OH
[[functional-group]]** attached to a hydrocarbon chain. The group is
coded in the name by the ending **−ol**, the third name-ending in
your [[iupac-nomenclature]] decoder (after *ane* for all-single bonds and *ene* for a double
bond). Methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol — the four small
members line up with the chain-length code counting carbons exactly
as before: *meth*, *eth*, *prop*. Ethanol is what everyday speech
just calls "alcohol" — the compound in alcoholic drinks — but in
chemistry the word names the whole family.

Position matters the moment chains reach three carbons. There are
**two different forms of propanol**: the −OH group can sit on the end
carbon of the chain (**propan-1-ol**) or on the second carbon
(**propan-2-ol**). The number works exactly like the alkene position
code from s07 — it names which carbon carries the group. And the two
forms are genuine **structural isomers**: there is no way to bend or
twist one molecule into the other, because moving an −OH group from
carbon 1 to carbon 2 means breaking bonds. Same molecular formula
(C₃H₈O), different structural formula — the s09 definition, live.

Extension, one step beyond the −OH pattern: a structural isomer of
propanol exists that contains **no −OH group at all** — CH₃OCH₂CH₃,
in which the oxygen atom sits *between* two carbon atoms instead of
being joined to a hydrogen. This compound is named methoxyethane and
belongs to a different homologous series, the **ethers**. It is a
quiet preview of the functional-group idea's power: one oxygen atom,
two different positions, two different families with different
chemistries.

:::key-point
Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol are structural isomers: the −OH group on
the end carbon versus the middle carbon. The position number in the
name does real structural work — it is the difference between two
compounds, not a stylistic variation, and the break-a-bond test
applies exactly as it did in s09.
:::

:::exam-hint
When you balance combustion equations for alcohols in the next
section, take care with the oxygen inside the molecule: the −OH
contributes an oxygen atom to the formula, and forgetting it is the
standard balancing error. Write the alcohol's formula first (ethanol
is C₂H₅OH, not C₂H₆), then balance — the extra O is inside the
reactant, and the equation arithmetic will expose it if you let it.
:::

:::misconception
"Propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol are the same compound — both are just
'propanol'." The name without the number is incomplete: the two
numbered forms place the −OH group on different carbons, which makes
them structural isomers with different structures. If an exam asks
you to draw "the two alcohols with formula C₃H₈O", the marking point
is the position of the group — end carbon versus middle carbon — and
a single unnumbered "propanol" answers neither.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you define the alcohols as a homologous series — functional
group, attachment point, name ending? Can you draw both propanols and
say why they are structural isomers rather than drawings of one
compound? Can you describe what makes methoxyethane different from
propan-1-ol despite the same molecular formula? Then you are ready
for the reactions that close the chapter.
:::

sections.title: Combustion, substitution and addition
sections.markdown:
The chapter closes its teaching with the third term of specification
4.6's toolkit in action: every organic reaction you meet at
International GCSE belongs to one of three classes — **combustion**,
**substitution** or **addition**. All organic compounds you will study
undergo combustion: it is just another word for burning, and it means
reaction with oxygen. Burn a [[hydrocarbon]] in **excess** oxygen and
the products are always carbon dioxide and water, together with a
large release of heat energy. Propane burning — the flame of a
camping stove, which is where propane is so often used — follows the
pattern:

C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l)

Butene burning shows the same shape with a different chain:

C₄H₈(g) + 6O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l)

Alcohols undergo similar reactions, and ethanol's equation is the one
to memorise:

C₂H₅OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l)

Balancing these is ordinary equation bookkeeping with one trap — the
oxygen atom already inside the alcohol (see the exam hint). The
products never change: complete combustion of anything organic in
excess oxygen gives CO₂ and H₂O, and the equations differ only in the
coefficients you need to balance carbon and hydrogen.

The other two classes are distinguished by what happens to the
reacting molecule. A **[[substitution-reaction]]** occurs when an atom
or group of atoms is **replaced** by a different atom or group —
something swaps in, something swaps out, and the molecule keeps its
overall shape. The standard example is a hydrogen atom in an alkane
being replaced by a halogen atom: ethane reacting with bromine gas
swaps one H for one Br,

CH₃CH₃ + Br₂ → CH₃CH₂Br + HBr

— bromoethane and hydrogen bromide as the two products. The detail
behind this reaction belongs to the alkanes chapter (u4:c24), but the
classification logic is complete here: count what entered and what
came out, and a replacement has happened.

An **[[addition-reaction]]** is the opposite gesture: something is
**added** to a molecule without taking anything away. Only unsaturated
molecules can do this, because the double bond carries spare bonding
capacity — and alkenes are the workhorses. Ethene reacting with
bromine takes the whole Br₂ molecule onto the two carbons:

CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br

One reactant set, **one** product — nothing is ejected, because
nothing needed replacing; the double bond simply opened and each
carbon took a bromine. Compare the two bromine reactions side by side
and the classification writes itself: ethane + bromine gives **two**
products (a substitution — the swapped-out hydrogen had to go
somewhere), ethene + bromine gives **one** (an addition). That
product-count contrast is the fastest classifier you own.

:::exam-hint
Specification wording for this section: *understand how to classify
reactions of organic compounds as substitution, addition and
combustion* — and the statement ends with a gift: **knowledge of
reaction mechanisms is not required**. You classify by observing what
happens (something burned? something swapped? something joined?),
never by explaining the electron-level how. Learn the three
one-sentence definitions, the product-count contrast for the two
bromine cases, and the three combustion equations, and 4.6 is fully
covered.
:::

:::misconception
"Ethane with bromine and ethene with bromine are the same reaction
because both use bromine." Same reactant fragment, different class.
Ethane is saturated — every bond is spoken for — so bromine can only
**replace** a hydrogen, and the displaced hydrogen leaves as HBr
(two products; substitution). Ethene is unsaturated — the C=C has
spare capacity — so the whole Br₂ **adds on** and nothing leaves (one
product; addition). Watch the products, not the reactants: what the
molecule does with the incoming atoms is the classification.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write the three combustion equations (propane, butene,
ethanol) and name the products of complete combustion in excess
oxygen? Can you define substitution and addition in one sentence
each, and classify the two ethane/ethene-plus-bromine reactions by
product count? Can you explain why alkenes but not alkanes undergo
addition? Those are the last teaching marks of the chapter — the
question bank is next.
:::

sections.title: Chapter 22 questions
sections.markdown:
You now hold the complete introductory toolkit for organic chemistry:
the [[hydrocarbon]] definition with its *only* discipline; the five
formula types and the jobs each one does; the [[homologous-series]] and
the [[functional-group]] that power them; the chain-length code and the
full decode procedure for names; structural [[isomerism]] with its
break-a-bond test; a first look at the alcohols; and the three
reaction classes with their classifier instincts. Every later organic
chapter — crude oil, alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, carboxylic acids,
esters, polymers — assumes these skills as standing equipment. The
question bank for this chapter joins the platform by the
specification points below, so every practice item you are served
targets exactly the machinery these sections built.

Before opening the bank, audit yourself against the chapter's core
moves. Can you run the two-element hydrocarbon audit and name the
compounds that stay outside the organic family? Can you move between
empirical, molecular, general, structural and displayed formulae —
including the CnH2n+2 arithmetic that generates a dodecane formula on
demand? Can you decode a six-carbon name into a structure and name a
structure from its code, branches and all? Can you enumerate the
three C₅H₁₂ isomers and explain why the phantom fourth is never
real? Can you classify any reaction the chapter can throw at you as
substitution, addition or combustion? Anything that wobbled is a
section to revisit, not a reason to start over.

The bank itself trains five question shapes. Naming-and-naming-back
items hand you condensed formulae to name and names to draw, from
one-carbon methane up to six-carbon chains and alcohols. Isomer
items ask for the definition, then for drawing and naming the sets —
the two isomers of C₄H₁₀, the five of C₆H₁₄, the double-bond set of
C₄H₈, and the stretch items that look beyond the −OH pattern. Formula
items test the ratio logic (empirical versus molecular) and the
general-formula arithmetic. Classification items present reactions
and demand [[substitution-reaction]], [[addition-reaction]] or combustion — with balanced
equations to write on the spot. And the analysis item pairs a
compound table with dot-and-cross drawing, displayed-formula drawing,
a general-formula recall and a full combustion equation. One warning
carried with the bank itself: some items deliberately reach slightly
beyond exam level — treat them as strength training, not as
evidence you are behind.

:::summary
- **Hydrocarbon (4.1)**: compound of hydrogen and carbon *only*; the
  two-element audit (carbon, hydrogen, nothing else) settles every
  membership question. Saturated = single C–C bonds only;
  unsaturated = contains double or triple C–C bonds.
- **Formula types (4.2)**: empirical = simplest whole-number ratio
  (calculable from data); molecular = actual atom counts (a whole-number
  multiple of the empirical formula; tells you nothing about joining);
  general = the whole family at once (alkanes CnH2n+2, alkenes CnH2n,
  alcohols CnH2n+2O); structural and displayed = the joining (all bonds
  drawn = displayed; not all = condensed structural).
- **Family terms (4.3)**: homologous series = similar chemistry from
  the same functional group, −CH₂− steps between members; functional
  group = the atom/group that determines chemical properties (−OH for
  alcohols, C=C for alkenes); isomerism = same molecular formula,
  different structural formulae.
- **IUPAC naming (4.4)**: names are codes — meth/eth/prop/but/pent/hex
  counts the longest chain; *ane*/*ene*/*ol* endings carry the bond
  and group information; branches are methyl/ethyl with position
  numbers from the smaller-numbers end; *di* marks a doubled branch.
- **Structures from formulae (4.5)**: enumerate isomers by varying
  chain length, branch positions, double-bond positions; discard
  rotations; C₅H₁₂ has exactly three isomers (pentane,
  2-methylbutane, 2,2-dimethylpropane).
- **Reaction classes (4.6)**: combustion = burn in oxygen → CO₂ + H₂O
  (three equations to know); substitution = replacement (alkane +
  halogen → two products); addition = joining onto C=C (alkene +
  halogen → one product). Mechanisms are not required.
:::

:::can-you
- Define a hydrocarbon with *only* in place, and say which four
  carbon-compound families stay outside organic chemistry?
- Write empirical, molecular and general formulae for the same
  compound, and explain what each one tells you?
- State the three-clause homologous-series definition and give the
  functional group of the alcohols and the alkenes?
- Decode 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene into a structure, and name the
  three C₅H₁₂ isomers from their structures?
- Draw propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol and say why both are C₃H₈O yet
  different compounds?
- Classify ethane-plus-bromine and ethene-plus-bromine by product
  count, and write the ethanol combustion equation?
:::

:::exam-hint
Every question in this bank maps to one of the six specification
points, all of them core: expect them in both Paper 1C and Paper 2C,
with naming/decoding and isomer enumeration the most frequent
mark-earners. The bank's own stretch note matters for your
temperature check: items flagged beyond exam level are there to build
technique, so a hard item is a signal to slow down and decode
systematically — never a signal that the exam will be like it. Drill
the decode procedure until it is boring; boredom is what fluency
feels like from the inside.
:::

:::misconception
"Isomer enumeration is guesswork — either you spot them or you don't."
Enumeration is a procedure: fix the molecular formula; walk chain
lengths from longest to shortest; at each length place branches (and
double bonds) at every distinct position; strike out anything
